questions.question: Which of the following banks was established in 1906?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Bank of India'.
  • The Bank of India was founded in 1906 in Mumbai. It later became one of the major nationalized banks in India.
  • It was founded in Mumbai (then Bombay) by a group of eminent businessmen, and it was privately owned until it was nationalized in 1969 along with 13 other major commercial banks in India.

questions.question: Which of the following banks was established in 1911 and was the first Indian commercial bank to be wholly owned and managed by Indians?
options: Alliance Bank of Shimla
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Central Bank of India'.
  • The Central Bank of India, founded in 1911, is notable for being the first commercial bank in India wholly owned and managed by Indians, making it a landmark in Indian banking history.
  • The bank was founded by Sir Sorabji Pochkhanawala, a visionary banker who believed in economic self-reliance and Indian entrepreneurship.
  • The eminent leader Sir Pherozeshah Mehta served as its first Chairman, lending credibility and national pride to the institution.
  • The founding of this bank marked a turning point in India’s financial history, as it demonstrated that Indians were capable of managing modern banking institutions on their own.

questions.question: In which year were the presidency banks Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras amalgamated to form the Imperial Bank of India?
questions.explanation:
• The Imperial Bank of India (IBI) was one of the oldest and largest commercial banks of the Indian subcontinent and was subsequently transformed into the State Bank of India in 1955.
  • Initially, as per its royal charter, it acted as the central bank for British India prior to the formation of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in 1935.
  • The Bank of Madras was one of the three Presidency Banks of British India, along with the Bank of Bengal and the Bank of Bombay.
  • It was established on 1 July 1843 through the amalgamation of a number of existing regional banks and was headquartered in Madras (now Chennai).
  • It was merged with the other presidential banks in 1921 to form the Imperial Bank of India, which later became the State Bank of India.
  • Founded: 27 January 1921; 101 years ago

Founder: John Maynard Keynes

Fate: Nationalization into State Bank of India in 1955

Successor: State Bank of India

Headquarters: Bombay, Bombay Presidency, British India

questions.question: Which of the following Instituitons was the first banking institution of India?
questions.explanation:
• In India, modern banking originated in the middle of the 18th century.
  • The first banking institution was the Bank of Hindustan established in 1770 and it was the first bank at Calcutta under European management. 
  • It was liquidated in 1830-32.

questions.question: The first Bank with limited liability managed by the Indian Board was Oudh Commercial Bank. It was established in 1881 at which place?
questions.explanation:
• Oudh Commercial Bank or Awadh Commercial Bank was an Indian bank established in 1881 in Faizabad and operated until 1958 when it failed.

  • It was the first commercial bank in India to have limited liability and an entirely Indian board of directors.

  • It was a small bank that had no branches and that served only local needs.

  • Type: Private Company

Industry: Banking

Founded: 1881

Defunct: 1958

Headquarters: Faizabad, India

  • Syndicate Bank

  • Corporation Bank
  • New Bank of India
  • Oriental Bank of Comm.
  • Punjab & Sind Bank
  • Vijaya Bank

questions.question: Where did the East India Company establish its initial presidency bank?
questions.explanation:
• The first presidency bank was Bank of Bengal, established in Calcutta.
  • The Bank of Bengal, founded on 2 June 1806, the Bank of Bombay, incorporated on 15 April 1840, and the Bank of Madras, established on 1 July 1843, constituted the Presidency Banks.
  • The Imperial Bank was predominantly privately owned, with 80% ownership in private hands, while the remaining shares were held by the state.

questions.question: Which of the following was the first Indian-owned commercial bank in India?
questions.explanation:
• Oudh Commercial Bank or Awadh Commercial Bank was an Indian bank established in 1881 in Faizabad and operated until 1958 when it failed. 
  • It was the first commercial bank in India having limited liability and an entirely Indian board of directors. 

Oldest commercial Bank

  • Bank of Calcutta is the oldest commercial bank in India. 
  • It was established in the year 1806. 
  • It was later renamed the Bank of Bengal. 
  • Currently it is known as State Bank of India.

questions.question: The Narasimham Committee submitted its report in the year _____.
questions.explanation:
• There was a need for an efficient banking system for a nation’s economic development.

  • In August 1991, the government appointed a 9-member committee called the Narasimham Committee to examine the functioning of banks.

  • Narasimham was the 13th governor of RBI, from 2nd May 1977 to 30th November 1977.

  • The committee submitted its report in December 1991 in the parliament.

questions.question: On which date the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India?
questions.explanation:
• Pursuant to the provisions of the State Bank of India Act of 1955, the Reserve Bank of
  • India, which is India's central bank, acquired a controlling interest in the Imperial Bank of India.
  • On 1 July 1955, the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India.
  • In 2008, the Government of India acquired the Reserve Bank of India's stake in SBI so as to remove any conflict of interest because the RBI
  • is the country's banking regulatory authority.
  • Founded: 1 July 1955
  • Headquarters: Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
  • Parent: Ministry of Finance (Government of India)

questions.question: What was the primary objective of the second phase of bank nationalization in India?
options: Expand the reach of social welfare programs
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'Expand the reach of social welfare programs.'
  • The second phase of bank nationalization aimed to ensure that the benefits of social welfare programs, such as agricultural credit and priority sector lending, reached a wider section of the population.

Key Info: 

1. First Phase (1969):

  • 14 major commercial banks were nationalized.

  • Objective: Direct banking resources towards agriculture, small industries, and priority sectors instead of just big industrialists.

2. Second Phase (1980):

  • 6 more private banks were nationalized (Punjab & Sind Bank, Vijaya Bank, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, and New Bank of India).

  • Main reason: Strengthen the government’s control over the banking system so that banks could be used as instruments for implementing social welfare programs, poverty alleviation schemes, and rural credit expansion.

3. Impact:

    • Ensured wider reach of banking services in semi-urban and rural areas.

    • Supported programs like IRDP (Integrated Rural Development Programme).

    • Boosted agricultural finance and rural development.

So, the second phase was less about competition or consolidation and more about aligning banks with the government’s socio-economic goals.

questions.question: The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance was also known as the________.
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India was set up on the basis of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance also known as the Hilton-Young Commission.

  • In 1926, Royal Commission on Indian Currency (Hilton Young Commission) recommends the establishment of a central bank to called the 'Reserve Bank of India'.

  • Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee revives the issue of the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India as the Central Bank for India.

questions.question: Which of the following banks was not nationalized in first phase of bank nationalization in 1969?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option (d) Punjab & Sindh Bank. 
  • Allahabad Bank, Bank of Baroda, Bank of India, Bank of Maharashtra, Central Bank of India, Canara Bank, Dena Bank, Indian Bank, Indian Overseas Bank, Punjab National Bank, Syndicate Bank, UCO Bank, Union Bank, United Bank of India were among the banks that were nationalized in 1969.
  • Further, six banks including 1. Andhra Bank; 2. Corporation Bank ; 3. New Bank of India; 4. Oriental Bank of Commerce; 5. Punjab & Sind Bank and 6. Vijaya Bank were nationalized in second phase of nationalization in 1980.

questions.question: When was the State Bank of India Nationalized?
questions.explanation:
• The State Bank of India (SBI) underwent nationalization in 1955 through the enactment of the SBI Act of 1955. 
  • Subsequently, the second phase of Indian bank nationalization occurred in 1980, involving the nationalization of seven additional banks with deposits exceeding 200 crores.

questions.question: In which year were the presidency banks Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras amalgamated to form the Imperial Bank of India?
questions.explanation:
• The Imperial Bank of India (IBI) was one of the oldest and largest commercial banks of the Indian subcontinent and was subsequently transformed into the State Bank of India in 1955.

  • Initially, as per its royal charter, it acted as the central bank for British India prior to the formation of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in 1935.

  • The Bank of Madras was one of the three Presidency Banks of British India, along with the Bank of Bengal and the Bank of Bombay.

  • It was established on 1 July 1843 through the amalgamation of a number of existing regional banks and was headquartered in Madras (now Chennai).

  • It was merged with the other presidential banks in 1921 to form the Imperial Bank of India, which later became the State Bank of India.

  • Founded: 27 January 1921; 101 years ago

Founder: John Maynard Keynes

Fate: Nationalization into State Bank of India in 1955

Successor: State Bank of India

Headquarters: Bombay, Bombay Presidency, British India

questions.question: Which of the following was the only public sector undertaking to be Nationalized in 1955?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option (e) state bank of India
  • Before 1969, only the State Bank of India was a public sector organisation and was nationalised in 1955.
  • In the background of the nationalisation of SBI, private banks were failing at a startlingly rapid rate.
  • Through the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969, the government of Indira Gandhi nationalised banks.
  • Fourteen significant private banks were nationalised, giving the government authority over them.

questions.question: Which bank was inaugrated by Mahatma Gandhi?
questions.explanation: Union Bank of India had opened it's 1st branch at Mumbai, Maharastra on November 1919. It was inaugrated by Mahatma Gandhi. On the eve of Independence there was only 4 branches of Union Bank of India.

questions.question: Which bank was the oldest joint stock bank in our country?
questions.explanation:
• Allahabad Bank was an Indian nationalized bank with its headquarters in Kolkata, India.
  • Founded in Allahabad in 1865 and nationalized by the government of India in 1969, the bank
  • provided banking and financial services for 155 years until it was merged with Indian Bank in
  • It was the oldest still running a joint stock bank in India until its merger.
  • Type: Public
  • Industry: Banking, Financial services
  • Founded: 24 April 1865; 157 years ago in
  • Allahabad, North-Western Provinces, British India
  • Defunct: 1 April 2020; 2 years ago
  • Fate: Merged with Indian Bank
  • Successor: Indian Bank
  • Headquarters: Kolkata, India

questions.question: When did the Banking Regulation Act come into effect?
questions.explanation:
• The Banking Regulation Act, of 1949 is a legislation in India that regulates all banking firms in India. Passed as the Banking Companies Act 1949, it came into force on 16 March 1949 and changed to Banking Regulation Act 1949 on 1 March 1966.
  • It is applicable in Jammu and Kashmir since 1956.
  • Initially, the law was applicable only to banking companies. But, in 1965 it was amended to make it applicable to cooperative banks and to introduce other changes.
  • In 2020 it was amended to bring the cooperative banks under the supervision of the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.question: NABARD was established on the recommendations of which committee?
questions.explanation:
• NABARD was established on the recommendations of B. Sivaraman Committee (by Act 61, 1981 of Parliament) on 12 July 1982 to implement the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act 1981.
  • It replaced the Agricultural Credit Department (ACD) and Rural Planning and Credit Cell (RPCC) of the Reserve Bank of India, and the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC).
  • National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) is an apex regulatory body for the overall regulation of regional rural banks and apex cooperative banks in India.
  • It is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance, Government of India.

questions.question: Which of the following committees recommended the formation of payment banks in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Nachiket Mor Committee.

  • In 2013, Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low-Income Households, headed by Nachiket Mor, was formed by the RBI.
  • In 2014, the Nachiket Mor committee submitted its final report.
  • Among its various recommendations, it recommended the formation of a new category of bank called payments bank.

questions.question: Which of the following committees recommended the formation of Gramin banks (RRBs) to provide the underprivileged population with enough credit?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is M. Narasimham Committee.

  • Narasimham’s working group, in the year 1975 recommended the formation of Gramin banks (RRBs) to provide the underprivileged population with enough credit.
  • An ordinance was passed in 1975, and in 1975, the RRB Act was passed, which legalized the status of RRBs.
  • The first RRB was created on 2nd October 1975, called the ‘Prathama Gramin Bank’.

questions.question: Which was the first bank in India to establish a savings account system?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Presidency Bank.

  • Presidency Bank was the first bank in India to establish a savings account system in 1833.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a motive behind the nationalization of banks in India?
options: Promoting foreign investments in the banking sector
All of the above were motives for nationalization
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is oprtion 'D' that is "Promoting foreign investments in the banking sector".
  • Promoting foreign investments in the banking sector was not a motive of Nationaliztion, in fact, the purpose of nationalization was opposite as Nationalization leads to  increase government ownership and control, not to encourage foreign participation.
  • Before 1969, private banks were unstable and catered only to big industries/urban elites. Nationalization brought them under government control and improved stability.
  • Agriculture, small industries, and weaker sections were neglected earlier. After nationalization, Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms were introduced.
  • A few industrial houses were controlling banking resources. Nationalization ensured that credit was distributed more fairly.
  • Therefore, all other options are the motives of Bank Nationalization.

questions.question: EXIM Bank was founded in which year?
questions.explanation:
Export-Import Bank was founded on 1Jan 1982 having the headquarter at Mumbai. It is owned by the Government of India. It also comes under Sec 45L and Sec 45N of RBI Act, 1934. 

EXIM Banks are special kind of financial institutions that provide wide range of financial assistance to the Exporters and Importers of a country.

questions.question: Who is often referred to as the father of banking reforms in India?
questions.explanation:
• Maidavolu Narasimham was an Indian banker who served as the 13th governor of the RBI from 2 May 1977 to 30 November 1977.

  • Due to his contributions to the banking and financial sector in India, he is often referred to as the father of banking reforms in India.

  • Some of his recommendations include changes to banking structures, the creation of asset recovery funds, the introduction of private sector banks, rural banking, technology upgradation and modernization of public sector banks, changes to capital adequacy and provisioning standards, and capital market-linked banking reforms.

questions.explanation:
• The Central Bank of India along with 13 other nationalized in 1969.
  • This move was aimed at bringing about social and economic reforms by promoting the government's control over the banking sector and channeling funds towards priority sectors like agriculture and small industries.

questions.question: Which of the following committees recommended the formation of payment banks in India?

  • In 2014, the Nachiket Mor committee submitted its final report. 
  • Among its various recommendations, it recommended the formation of a new category of bank called payments bank.

questions.question: How did bank nationalization impact the banking sector in India?
options: Enhanced access to banking services in rural areas
Strengthened the public sector presence in the banking sector
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is (e) All of the above.
  • Bank nationalization had a significant impact on the Indian banking sector.
  • It increased competition, expanded access to banking services, improved efficiency, and strengthened the public sector's role in banking.

questions.question: What was the primary objective of bank nationalization in India?
options: Improve access to banking services in rural areas
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is (c) Improve access to banking services in rural areas.
  • Despite the Banking Regulation Act of 1949, substantially fewer loans were given to small businesses and rural areas than to large companies. Commercial bank loans to industries increased from 34% to 68% between 1951 and 1968, nearly double the amount given to agriculture, which got less than 2% of the credit.
  • Therefore, it is imperative to nationalize the commercial banks.
  • The nationalization of banks aimed to bring banking services to the masses, especially in rural and semi-urban areas, and promote financial inclusion.

questions.question: Which bank is the first bank purely managed by Indians, which was established in Lahore in 1895?
questions.explanation:
• The first bank purely managed by Indians was Punjab National Bank, established in Lahore in 1895.

  • The Punjab National Bank has not only survived to date but is also one of the largest banks in India.

  • Punjab National Bank (abbreviated as PNB) is an Indian public sector bank headquartered in Delhi.

  • The bank was founded in May 1894 and is the second largest government-owned bank in India, both in terms of its business volumes and its network.

  • Founded: 19 May 1894

Founder: Dyal Singh Majithia, Lala Lajpat Rai

Headquarters: Dwarka, Delhi, India

Non-Exe Chairman: K G Ananthakrishnan

MD & CEO: Atul Kumar Goel

questions.question: How many major banks were nationalized in the first phase of bank nationalization in India?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is (c) 14.
  • On July 19, 1969, the 14 biggest commercial banks were nationalised by the Indira Gandhi administration under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969.
  • The majority of the bank deposits were held by these lenders. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertaking) Bill was approved by the president on August 9 after being passed by the parliament.

questions.question: Who headed the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC) established in 2011?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Justice B. N. Srikrishna'.
  • The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC), formed in 2011, was chaired by Justice B. N. Srikrishna.
  • Its primary goal was to review and restructure the legal and regulatory framework of India’s financial sector.
  • The FSLRC aimed to review existing financial laws and restructure the
  • The FSLRC’s reform scope included consolidation and streamlining of laws related to banking, insurance, securities, and pensions, aiming for a unified financial regulatory structure.m to create a more unified and efficient framework governing the financial sector in India.

questions.question: The Narasimham Committee II wanted the banks to reduce their NPAs to _____ by 2002.
questions.explanation:
• The Narasimham Committee II, also known as the Banking Sector Committee, was tasked with reviewing the progress of the implementation of reforms and suggesting ways to further strengthen the sector.

  • The committee wanted the banks to reduce NPAs to 3% by 2002.

  • It also recommended the formation of Asset Reconstruction Companies. It was these recommendations that led to the introduction of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, of 2002.

questions.question: What capital adequacy ratio did the Narasimham-II Committee target for banks by the year 2000?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option 'B'.
  • The Narasimham-II Committee was appointed in 1991 to address the issues of banking reform and consolidation in India.
  • It recommended raising the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of banks, which measures a financial institution's ability to absorb losses, to 9% by the year 2000.
  • This objective was aimed at improving the stability and resilience of the banking sector.

questions.question: Which of the following committee was established to scrutinize the application for new banks in India?
questions.explanation:
• Bimal Jalan Committee on New Bank Licenses submitted its report to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on 25 February 2014.

  • RBI constituted the committee under the chairmanship of Bimal Jalan in October 2013.

  • RBI had constituted the committee to examine the criteria, business plans, and corporate governance practices of applicants applying for new bank Licenses.

  • It recommended ‘in-principle approval’ of banking licenses to Bandhan microfinance and IDFC (Infrastructure Development and Finance Corporation).

questions.question: The Nandkarni Committee recommended procedures based on ______.
options: Transactions in Public Sector bonds and Mutual Funds
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), set up the Nandkarni Committee in 1992. The purpose of the Committee was to evolve an improved procedure for conducting transactions in public sector bonds (PSU Bonds) and units of mutual funds.
  • The Committee was set up in pursuance of one of the recommendations of the Committee to enquire into the Securities Transactions of Banks and Financial Institutions (popularly known as Janakiraman Committee).
  • The terms of reference for the Committee required it to evolve improved procedures based on the examination of the existing procedures for transactions in PSU bonds and units mentioned above to eliminate deficiencies including those in the practice of issuing bankers' receipts.
  • The Committee was required to recommend modalities of an alternative system covering the booking of transactions and efficient methods of accounting and transfers.

questions.question: What was the primary goal of the Sukhmoy Chakravarty Committee established in 1982?
options: To establish guidelines for the establishment of Private Sector Banks
To contemplate the amalgamation of all cooperative banks
To evaluate the functioning of the Indian Monetary system
To streamline the functioning of Rural Banks
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option ‘C’ that is ‘To evaluate the functioning of the Indian Monetary system.’
  • The Sukhmoy Chakravarty Committee was formed to assess and enhance the performance of the monetary system in India.

questions.question: The Narasimham Committee was appointed for reforms in which sector?
questions.explanation: The Narasimham Committee was appointed for reforms in the banking sector. It submitted two reports, known as Narasimham Committee I (1991) and Narasimham Committee II (1997), which made comprehensive recommendations for strengthening and modernizing the Indian banking system.

questions.question: Which of the following committee was constitute by RBI to re-examine the existing classification and suggest revised guidelines with regard to priority Sector Lending(PSL)?
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank had constituted the Committee under the chairmanship of Shri. M. V. Nair on August 25, 2011 pursuant to the announcement made in the Monetary Policy Statement 2011-12.

  • The Committee was to re-examine the existing classification and suggest revised guidelines with regard to priority sector lending and related issues.

  • The Committee had 10 Members from diverse fields and Dr. Deepali Pant Joshi, CGM-in-Charge, Rural Planning and Credit Department, Reserve Bank of India was its Member Secretary.

  • The recommendations of the Committee are expected to have significant impact in addressing issue of directing lending to those who have lack of access to credit and to those sectors which generate large employment.

  • Priority Sector was defined for the first time in 1972 by Dr. K S Krishnaswamy Committee.

  • In order to examine and finalize the draft regulations for Collective Investment schemes, SEBI appointed Dave committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. S. A. Dave.

  • AK Bhuchar Committee was set up for coordination Between Term Lending Institutions And Commercial Banks

questions.question: Which committee was set up by the RBI in 2022 to review the regulatory framework for non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs)?
options: RBI Internal Working Group on NBFIs
questions.explanation:
• The RBI Internal Working Group on NBFIs was set up in 2022 to review the regulatory framework for non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) in India. The group was chaired by Dr. M. K. Jain, former Deputy Governor of the RBI.
  • The group submitted its report in June 2023, and made a number of recommendations for strengthening the regulatory framework for NBFIs. These recommendations include:
    • Introducing a risk-based approach to regulation for NBFIs
    • Creating a unified regulatory framework for all NBFIs
    • Strengthening the oversight of NBFIs by the RBI
    • Improving the transparency and disclosure requirements for NBFIs
    • The RBI has said that it will take appropriate action on the recommendations of the group.

questions.question: The Raghuram Rajan Committee was formed for which of the following purposes?
questions.explanation:
• The Raghuram Rajan Committee was constituted by the Government of India in 2007 for proposing financial sector reforms in India.

  • In the report of the committee, which was titled A Hundred Small Steps, recommendations were of broad-based reforms across the financial sector. The committee argued that India should take “a hundred small steps” instead of focusing "on a few large, and usually politically controversial steps".

questions.question: Which of the following committee recommended improving customer service in the banks?
questions.explanation:
• The Goiporia Committee was set up in 1990 by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

  • The Goiporia committee aimed at exploring and giving recommendations for improving customer service in the banks.

  • The Goiporia committee made several recommendations in its report for all the banks across India and expressed a need to keep a customer complaint book so that the issues that the customers used to face can be documented properly, and the proper measures for those problems can be taken.

questions.question: Which banking sector reform committees are related to Regional Rural Banks?
questions.explanation:
• The Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were first set up on 2 October 1975 (only 5 in number) to take banking services to the doorsteps of the rural masses, especially in the remote areas with no access to banking services with twin responsibilities to provide credit to the weaker sections of the society at concessional rate of interest who earlier depended on private money lending and to mobilize rural savings and channelize them for helping constructive activities in the rural areas.
  • The Working Group on RRBs (Kelkar Committee) in 1984 recommended that small and uneconomic RRBs be merged in the interest of economic viability.
  • Following the suggestions of the Kelkar Committee, the government stopped opening new RRBs in 1987-by that time their total number stood at 196.
  • Due to excessive leaningstowardssocial banking and catering to the highly economically weaker sections, these banks started incurring huge losses by the early 1980s.

questions.question: Which committee was set up by the RBI in 2020 to review the financial stability framework in India?
questions.explanation:
• The Nandan Nilekani Committee was set up by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in January 2019 to recommend measures for deepening digital payments in India. The committee submitted its report in May 2019, and one of its key recommendations was the introduction of a unified payment interface (UPI).
  • The UPI is a real-time payment system that allows users to transfer money between bank accounts instantly using their mobile phones. It is a single platform that can be used for both person-to-person (P2P) and person-to-merchant (P2M) payments.
  • The UPI has been a major success in India, and it has helped to accelerate the growth of digital payments in the country. As of March 2023, the UPI has processed over 50 billion transactions worth more than ₹30 trillion.

questions.question: Which of the following committee was established to scrutinize the application for new banks in India?
questions.explanation:
• Bimal Jalan Committee on New Bank Licenses submitted its report to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on 25 February 2014.
  • RBI constituted the committee under the chairmanship of Bimal Jalan in October 2013.
  • RBI had constituted the committee to examine the criteria, business plans, and corporate governance practices of applicants applying for new bank Licenses.
  • It recommended ‘in-principle approval’ of banking licenses to Bandhan microfinance and IDFC (Infrastructure Development and Finance Corporation).

questions.question: Which of the following committee was set up to curb illegal transactions on Government Securities by banks?
questions.explanation:
• The Janakiraman Committee was set up in 1992.

  • This committee aimed to investigate the number of market irregularities that had risen and were harshly damaging the banking system in the country.

  • Some banks were undertaking large-scale transactions in Government securities through the medium of brokers in the course of which they were violating the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'s detailed guidelines.

  • The Janakiraman Committee Report examined all these aspects and included the reasons for these irregularities.

  • The repo rates and their growth were strange and cautioned the RBI to fear some unwanted financial growth.

questions.question: Which of the following committee recommended Loans to IRDP(Integrated Rural Development Program) beneficiaries?
questions.explanation:
• An Expert Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri D.R. Mehta, Deputy Governor, was constituted by RBI on the 29th of September 1993.
  • The purpose was to review the Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and to recommend suitable measures for strengthening it to make it more effective in the alleviation of poverty.
  • The Committee was able to collect a mass of statistical data and other information on the issues involved.
  • It recommended loans to IRDP(Integrated Rural Development Program) beneficiaries.

questions.question: Which Committee's recommendation led to the formation of NABARD in 1982?
questions.explanation:
• Sivaramman Committee recommended the formation of NABARD. NABARD was established on 12 July 1982 to implement the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act 1981.
  • The Committee was formed on 30 March 1979, under the Chairmanship of Shri B. Sivaraman, former Member of the Planning Commission, Government of India.
  • The Committee’s interim report, submitted on 28 November 1979, outlined the need for a new organizational device for providing undivided attention, forceful direction, and pointed focus to credit-related issues linked with rural development.
  • Its recommendation was the formation of a unique development financial institution that would address these aspirations and the creation of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was approved by Act 61, 1981 of the Parliament.

questions.question: Which of the following committee appointed by the Government of India recommended the formation of lead banks in 1969?
questions.explanation:
• A Committee of Bankers on Branch Expansion Programme of public sector banks appointed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Chairmanship of Shri F. K. F. Nariman (Nariman Committee) endorsed the idea of the area approach in its report (November 1969).

  • It recommended that to enable the public sector banks to discharge their social responsibilities, each bank should concentrate on certain districts where it should act as a 'Lead Bank'.

  • According to the above recommendations, the Lead Bank Scheme was introduced by Reserve Bank in December 1969.

  • The Scheme emphasized making specific banks in each district the key instruments of local development by entrusting them with the responsibility of locating growth centers, assessing deposit potential, identifying credit gaps, and evolving a coordinated approach to credit deployment in each district, in concert with other banks and credit agencies.

questions.question: Which of the following committee recommended that the public sector bank should be free and autonomous?
questions.explanation:
• The Narasimham Committee II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms) was tasked with conducting a progress review of the implementation of banking reforms since 1998, to further strengthen India's financial institutions.
  • It concentrated on issues such as bank size and capital adequacy ratios, among other things.
  • According to the Narasimham committee, government ownership and management of banks do not increase autonomy and flexibility in the operation of public sector banks.
  • Greater autonomy was proposed for the public sector banks for them to function withequivalent professionalism as their international counterparts.
  • For this, the panel recommended that recruitment procedures, training, and remuneration policies of public sector banks be brought in line with the best-market practices of professional banking systems.

questions.question: Which of the following was a key impact of banking liberalization in India?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Entry of private sector banks'.
  • Banking liberalization in the 1990s allowed the entry of new private sector banks like HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank.
  • This brought competition, improved service quality, and modern technology.
  • Nationalization was a pre-liberalization policy (1969, 1980), while SLR was reduced after liberalization.

questions.question: When was RN Malhotra Committee set up to make recommendations related to the reforms in the insurance sector?
questions.explanation:
• The RN Malhotra Committee was set up in 1993 to make recommendations related to the reforms in the insurance sector.
  • The committee submitted its report in 1994 and suggested the inclusion of private players in the insurance industry, and also suggested the allowance of foreign companies to enter the sector.
  • This committee also recommended the constitution of IRDA as an autonomous body for the regulation and development of the insurance sector.

questions.question: What was the main recommendation of the Narsimhan Committee-II in 1998?
options: It recommended merging banks and financial institutions, NBFCs, etc. based on synergy and operational efficiency.
It recommended doing away with the Priority Sector Lending system.
questions.explanation:
• Narasimham Committee- II is also known as the Banking Sector Committee.
  • This Committee aimed to review the progress of the implementation of reforms and to suggest a design for further strengthening the sector.
  • The Committee recommended the merger of major public sector banks to boost international trade. However, the Committee warned against merging stronger banks with weaker banks.
  • It recommended merging banks and financial institutions, NBFCs, etc. based on synergy and operational efficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines Privatization in the context of Indian banking reforms?
options: Transfer of ownership from public to private sector
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'Transfer of ownership from public to private sector'.
  • Privatization means shifting ownership and management from the public sector to the private sector. In banking, it refers to reducing government stake in public sector banks (PSBs) below 51%, allowing private players to control operations, improve efficiency, and bring innovation.

questions.question: What does the acronym "CAMEL" stand for in banking performance evaluation?
options: Capital Adequacy, Asset Quality, Management Efficiency, Earnings Quality, Liquidity
Cash Adequacy, Asset Liquidity, Management Level, Equity, Leverage
Credit Allocation, Asset Management, Market Exposure, Earnings, Liability
Capital Allocation, Asset Control, Market Efficiency, Equity, Liquidity
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' that is 'Capital Adequacy, Asset Quality, Management Efficiency, Earnings Quality, Liquidity'.
  • The CAMEL framework is used by regulatory bodies like the RBI and international banking supervisors to assess the overall health and performance of banks. The parameters are:

  • C – Capital Adequacy: Measures a bank’s ability to absorb losses (Basel norms are relevant here).

  • A – Asset Quality: Evaluates the quality of loans and investments, focusing on NPAs.

  • M – Management Efficiency: Assesses the competence and effectiveness of the bank’s management.

  • E – Earnings Quality: Measures profitability and income stability.

  • L – Liquidity: Examines the bank’s ability to meet short-term obligations.

questions.question: Who among the following chaired RBI's expert committee to review the governance of boards in India?
questions.explanation:
Dr P.J. Nayak chaired RBI's expert committee to review the governance of boards in India.

The Expert Committee was requested to examine the working of banks’ boards including whether the adequate time is devoted to issues of strategy, growth, governance and risk management; to review central bank regulatory guidelines on bank ownership, ownership concentration and representation in the board.

questions.question: Globalization in the banking sector led to:
options: Entry and expansion of foreign banks in India
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Entry and expansion of foreign banks in India'.
  • Globalization refers to greater integration with the world economy.
  • In the Indian banking context, foreign banks like Citibank, HSBC, and Standard Chartered expanded their operations, bringing in international practices and competition.
  • This was facilitated by the post-1991 economic reforms.

questions.question: The 4R Framework was introduced in 2017 as a government strategy to tackle the mounting Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) or bad loans that were weakening India's banking system. Which of the following is NOT one of the components of the 4R Framework?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is 'Revaluation'.
  • The 4R Framework was introduced in 2017 as a government strategy to tackle the mounting Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) or bad loans that were weakening India's banking system.
  • The four components of the 4R Framework are:

  1. Recognition of NPAs

  2. Recapitalization of banks

  3. Resolution of stressed assets

  4. Reforms in governance and efficiency
    "Revaluation" is not part of this framework.

questions.question: What is the full form of 'LPG' in the context of Indian economic reforms of 1991?
questions.explanation:
• The cocrrect answer is option 'B' that is 'Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization'.
  • In the context of Indian economic reforms, LPG stands for Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization. These were the three pillars of the 1991 economic reforms introduced to revive the Indian economy from a balance of payments crisis.
  • Liberalization: Reducing government control and encouraging private sector participation.
  • Privatization: Transferring ownership of public sector enterprises to private hands.
  • Globalization: Integrating the Indian economy with the global economy through trade, investment, and technology.
